source.title: Steering Large Language Model Activations in Sparse Spaces
source.authors: Reza Bayat; Ali Rahimi-Kalahroudi; Mohammad Pezeshki; A. P. Sarath Chandar; Pascal Vincent

record.tranche_reason: The study varies SAE dictionary width, but measures SAS-vector sparsity, raw active-feature counts, and steering performance—not whether larger-dictionary features correspond to, partition, or lie near smaller-dictionary features. It does not test any listed version.
record.gate_note: Section 4.4.1 reports SAE-width effects on feature counts and steering performance. These are related to SAE scaling but do not measure feature splitting or its proposed geometric and input-coverage relationships, so they are recorded under fits_no_version. Other steering and benchmark results do not test the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study proposes Sparse Activation Steering and varies Gemma Scope SAE width (16K–1M). It measures only the count of features in its behavior-steering vectors, raw active-feature counts, and steering performance. It never matches latents across dictionary sizes, checks input coverage or decoder-direction similarity, examines feature families, absorption, or decomposition, or compares training objectives. Its results therefore do not bear on any version. Fewer SAS features at larger width is a method-specific count, not evidence of splitting.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that scaling SAE width makes SAS vectors sparser, which they read as improved monosemanticity. They report positive steering as preserved and negative steering as slightly degraded at higher τ.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses pretrained JumpReLU SAEs and its own contrastive Sparse Activation Steering method. It analyzes scaling through SAS-vector sparsity and steering performance, not through feature matching or split detection.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported sparsity trend is strongest at higher τ; steering performance is reported as stable for positive steering and slightly degraded for negative steering at higher τ.

fits_no_version.finding: For Gemma-2 2B Gemma Scope SAEs, the number of features in SAS behavior vectors falls as width grows from 16K to 1M, most clearly at τ=0.9. Raw active-feature counts stay roughly stable.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Wider SAEs concentrate contrastive behavior-specific features into fewer latents passing a consistency threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed λ=±1, positive steering is stable across widths; negative steering degrades slightly at higher τ.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steering with sparse vectors from wider SAEs keeps positive-steering efficacy at fixed strength.

record.problems: The width-scaling results are reported qualitatively in text and plotted in figures; uncertainty estimates are not stated. The measurements do not directly test the feature-level splitting claim.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported result measures feature splitting or a listed version. General steering evaluations, open-ended generations, and benchmark results were not extracted because they do not test the claim versions.

untested.parts: No matching of latents across sizes, no input-coverage test, no directional similarity.
Uses open Gemma Scope SAEs, but performs no splitting analysis.
No feature families or hierarchy geometry.
No parent/child firing or absorption analysis.
No decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents, and no count of novel latents.

missing.what: Behavior-pair feature-overlap counts at 65K vs 1M width (fewer total features at 1M). Not splitting evidence, but a width comparison a researcher might want.

record.verdict_notes: The authors equate 'fewer active SAS features' with monosemanticity. This interpretation is not a splitting measurement. Uncertainty is not reported, and values appear only in figures.

versions.untested_parts: No feature matching across dictionary sizes, input partition or coverage, or directional similarity.
No test of splitting across models or open SAE releases.
No nested feature families, geometric closeness, or concept-hierarchy test.
No parent-child firing or absorption analysis, or test of whether size or sparsity fixes it.
No decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents or analysis of novel latents.
No comparison of SAE training objectives or test of whether the objective produces splitting.

rows.subject: Gemma-2 2B

rows.measure: Number of active features in SAS vectors (sparsity).
rows.value: Figure 7; the text states that increasing width increases SAS-vector sparsity, particularly at τ = 0.9.
rows.note: The text reports a qualitative trend; numerical values are shown only in the figure. This feature-count measure does not establish feature splitting or correspondence.
rows.check: Counts SAS-vector features after the study's own τ filtering and common-feature removal. This is a property of the study's method, not a coarse-to-fine split of features across dictionary sizes. The 'none' link is correct.

rows.note: The text reports a qualitative trend; numerical values are shown only in the figure. Stable active-feature counts do not establish splitting or input coverage.
rows.check: Average raw L0 across widths; says nothing about whether features split. The 'none' link is correct.

rows.note: The text reports a qualitative comparison; numerical values are shown only in the figure. Steering performance does not measure feature splitting.
